explanations.explanation: Assyria it is, friend. God says, “Look at Assyria, a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches that shaded the forest.” So the first tree in this message is a whole nation dressed up as a cedar. I think Pharaoh is being told to take a good, long look.

Babylon is a name you may know, but it doesn't show up anywhere in these verses. God says, “Look at Assyria, a cedar in Lebanon…” Assyria is the nation pictured as the cedar. Good guess, though, friend.

Moab isn't named in this passage, friend. The nation pictured as the cedar is Assyria. God says, “Look at Assyria, a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches that shaded the forest.” Keep that name handy, because this tree matters in the rest of the message.

Water, water, WATER! God says, “The waters made it grow; the deep springs made it tall…” Those springs sent their streams all around its base. This tree had a serious water supply, and it grew like it knew it.
Soil is a fair guess, since trees do love dirt. But the text never mentions it here. God says, “The waters made it grow; the deep springs made it tall…” The water gets the credit in this verse.

Nice thought, but the sun doesn't come up in this verse. Lebanon is where the cedar stands, and that's all the text says about it there. God says, “The waters made it grow; the deep springs made it tall…” Water gets the credit.
Shade, baker! The text says, “all the great nations lived in its shade.” Think of a tree so big that whole nations set up under it. That's a lot of folks sharing one patch of cool.

Hollow is a creative pick, but the text never says anything about a hollow. It says “all the great nations lived in its shade.” The nations were under the branches, not tucked inside the trunk. That's one crowded tree otherwise.

Roots do show up in this passage, just not here. In verse 7, its roots extended to abundant waters. For the nations, the verse says, “all the great nations lived in its shade.” The shade is where they lived.

The text says the opposite. God says, “The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it…” The cypresses couldn't compare with its branches, and the plane trees couldn't match its boughs. No tree in the garden of God could compare with its beauty.

False is right, friend. God says, “The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it…” The cypresses couldn't compare with its branches, and the plane trees couldn't match its boughs. This tree had no competition.

True, baker! God says, “I made it beautiful with its many branches…” So the beauty didn't start with the tree. God is the one who says He made it beautiful. Hold onto that, because it matters for what's coming.
It's actually true. God says, “I made it beautiful with its many branches…” He says it Himself, in the same verse where the trees of Eden envy the cedar. So the beauty is something God says He gave.

explanations.answer: It grew proud of its height
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. God says the cedar “…grew proud on account of its height…” After all those verses of praise, this is the line that turns the whole message. Beautiful branches were never the problem, and the text puts the pride right next to the height.

I get why you'd pick it, since this tree was HUGE. But the text never says it crowded anyone out. What it says is that the cedar “…grew proud on account of its height…” That's what God holds against it.

explanations.answer: It drank up all the water
explanations.explanation: Water is all over this story, but nobody accuses the cedar of drinking it all. Earlier, God says the waters made it grow (Ezekiel 31:4). The charge in verse 10 is that the cedar “…grew proud on account of its height…” Pride is the problem here.

The text says the opposite. After the cedar is cut down, “…all the peoples of the earth left its shade and abandoned it.” They left, so they aren't staying. That's a quiet, sad moment for a tree that had the great nations living in its shade.
False is right. The text says, “And all the peoples of the earth left its shade and abandoned it.” Remember how the great nations lived in that shade earlier? Now they're gone.
On the fallen trunk, baker. The text says, “All the birds of the air nested on its fallen trunk…” The tree is lying down now. That's a big change from the high branches.
Mountains do come up in this passage, but not for the nests. The branches have fallen on the mountains (Ezekiel 31:12). The birds, though, “…nested on its fallen trunk…”
The clouds are where the cedar's top used to be, back in verse 3. The text doesn't put the birds there, though. It says they “…nested on its fallen trunk…” That's the tree lying down, friend.

The text says the opposite. God says, “This happened so that no other trees by the waters would become great in height and set their tops among the clouds…” So the point of the cedar's fall isn't more tall trees. It's the opposite.

False is right. God says, “This happened so that no other trees by the waters would become great in height and set their tops among the clouds…” The other trees aren't meant to follow that path. This is a heavy part, so I'll let the words stand.
Yes, baker. The text says, “…all the trees of the field fainted because of it.” God also says He made Lebanon mourn for it. The trees of the field are reacting to the fall.
The text doesn't say that. It says, “…all the trees of the field fainted because of it.” God also says He made Lebanon mourn for it. The verse tells us they react to the fall by fainting.
The verse goes the other way. God says He made Lebanon mourn for the cedar, and “…all the trees of the field fainted because of it.” That's mourning, not celebrating.
Quake, friend. God says, “I made the nations quake at the sound of its downfall…” The sound of the downfall is what sets them quaking. God is the One who made it happen.
Cheering isn't in the verse, baker. God says, “I made the nations quake at the sound of its downfall…” That's shaking, not celebrating. The sound of the downfall is what moves the nations.
No singing here, friend. The text says, “I made the nations quake at the sound of its downfall…” The sound of the downfall is what shakes them. They quake instead.
Allies, baker! The text says, “As its allies they had lived in its shade among the nations.” So these trees were its allies, living under the same big branches. They went down with it.
The verse doesn't call them strangers. It says, “As its allies they had lived in its shade among the nations.” They're called its allies, and they lived in its shade.
The text never calls them saplings. It says, “As its allies they had lived in its shade among the nations.” So they're allies, not little ones the cedar planted.

True. God says to Pharaoh, “You also will be brought down to the depths of the earth to be with the trees of Eden.” The message started with Pharaoh's greatness and ends with Pharaoh himself. The text says it plainly.
It's actually true. God says, “You also will be brought down to the depths of the earth to be with the trees of Eden.” The line is spoken right to Pharaoh. The words just stand.
